rv.q: The result is provocative but messy...But cumbersome as it is, 'The Refuge Plays' suggests the potential for stories to exceed the world's limitations.
Nathan Alan Davis has put together a three-part drama full of engaging small gestures that fail to add up.
Davis's warm, affectionate evening is something of a refuge from the clank and clatter and confusion of a lot of contemporary playwrighting.
'The Refuge Plays' is a joy ride worth taking.
Davis, for the most part, has given us characters that we can easily fall in love with, each with their own path to refuge.

Three and a half hours is a long time to sit but The Refuge Plays offers rewards to those patient enough to make it through to the end, especially for Parker’s transformative performance of Early from grouchy matriarch to self-determined young woman.
This top-flight cast is strong enough to occasionally distract you from the cumulative impression of witnessing an epic that is a mile wide but only an inch deep.
The Refuge Plays is also, at times, meandering, slow, confusing, tedious, and emotionally distant.
Unfortunately, the play's inconsistencies stand in the way of its success. With a runtime of three-and-a-half hours, the play takes much too long to get to where it needs to go.
It is an overcrowded, aria-packed piece so awkwardly constructed that it almost seems designed to thwart drama altogether.
There's a comfortableness with each character's idiosyncrasies that the cast creates that draws the audience into the incredulousness of the play and provides an evening of warmth and belonging.
She's an indomitable force of nature, and her journey is a rewarding one.
Davis's greatest accomplishment in 'The Refuge Plays' lies in the creation of engaging, warm-blooded, intensely human characters for whom we come to care deeply.
